successors.name: Habsburg monarchy
successors.text: the southern part with Krnov, Bruntál, Fulnek and Opava, which stayed Austrian

ledger.x: 1269: Ottokar II of Bohemia carves the lordship of Opava out of the Margraviate of Moravia for his natural son Nicholas I, 'split off from the Margraviate of Moravia before 1269'; Nicholas first appears as 'Lord of Opava' in 1269.

1318: 'Opava was officially raised to a duchy in 1318', confirmed as a fief for Nicholas II (Bohemian vassal since 1327 for Racibórz; the lordship had been pawned to Bolesław III in 1310-1311 and 'redeemed by King John of Bohemia in 1311').
1377: 'Duke John I again separated Opava from the duchies of Racibórz and Krnov'; Opava was granted to his younger brothers.

1485: 'Victor in turn had to cede it to the Bohemian anti-king Matthias Corvinus in 1485' (George of Poděbrady had given it to his son Victor in 1465); Matthias installed his illegitimate son John as duke.

1506: 'King Vladislas II Jagiellon of Bohemia granted Opava to Duke Casimir II of Cieszyn', held to 1528; in 1521 'the Opava line of the Přemyslids had finally become extinct' and the duchy fell back to the Bohemian Crown, from 1526 Habsburg.
1614: Prince Karl I of Liechtenstein 'was invested with the Duchy of Troppau in 1614' by Emperor Matthias; in 1620 he acquired the Duchy of Krnov.
1742: 'In 1742, in the course of the First Silesian War and the Treaty of Breslau, the Duchy was divided once more.'

1742: the southern part 'including Krnov, Bruntál, Fulnek and Opava, stayed in Austrian Silesia' (a crown land of the Austrian Empire from 1804); the Austrian Duchy of Troppau ceased to exist in 1918.

wars.name: First Silesian War
wars.outcome: The Treaty of Breslau of 1742 divided the duchy: the northern part to Prussia, the southern part stayed Austrian.

certainty.note: The page names towns, not boundaries.
The Treaty of Breslau divided the duchy; the page names the towns each side kept.
